3	description: Learn how to enable the cacheComponents flag in Next.js.
4	related:
5	  links:
6	    - app/getting-started/caching
7	    - app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration-cache-components
8	    - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache
9	    - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote
10	---
11	
12	Cache Components enables component and function-level caching using the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive. Data fetching is dynamic by default, and you choose what to cache at the page, component, or function level. Next.js prerenders a static HTML shell that is served immediately while dynamic content streams in when ready, letting you mix static and dynamic content within a single route.
13	
14	## Usage
15	
16	To enable the `cacheComponents` flag, set it to `true` in your `next.config.ts` file:
17	
18	```ts filename="next.config.ts"
19	import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
20	
21	const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
22	  cacheComponents: true,
23	}
24	
25	export default nextConfig
26	```
27	
28	> **Good to know**: Cache Components requires the Node.js runtime. Migrate any routes that set the deprecated `runtime = 'edge'` export, and note that other server-side JavaScript runtimes are not guaranteed to work. See [Migrating to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components#runtime--edge).
29	
30	When `cacheComponents` is enabled, you can use the following cache functions and configurations:
31	
32	- The [`use cache` directive](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache)
33	- The [`cacheLife` function](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife) with `use cache`
34	- The [`cacheTag` function](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag)
35	
36	> **Good to know**: If you used `experimental.useCache` or `experimental.dynamicIO`, migrate using the [Version 16 upgrade guide](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#experimentaldynamicio-and-experimentalusecache). To migrate route segment configs and other caching patterns, see [Migrating to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components).
37	
38	Additionally, `cacheComponents` implements **[Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/glossary#partial-prerendering-ppr)** as the default behavior in the App Router. This means the `experimental.ppr` configuration flag and the `experimental_ppr` route segment configuration are no longer necessary and have been removed.
39	
40	Read [Prerendering](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#prerendering) for how the static shell and streaming fit together.
41	
42	> **Good to know**: If you used experimental PPR in Next.js 15, refer to the [Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#partial-prerendering-ppr) section of the Version 16 upgrade guide when migrating.
43	
44	## Navigation with Activity
45	
46	When `cacheComponents` is enabled, Next.js uses React's [`<Activity>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity) component to preserve component state during client-side navigation.
47	
48	Rather than unmounting the previous route when you navigate away, Next.js sets the Activity mode to [`"hidden"`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity#activity). This means:
49	
50	- Component state is preserved when navigating between routes
51	- When you navigate back, the previous route reappears with its state intact
52	- Effects are cleaned up when a route is hidden, and recreated when it becomes visible again
53	
54	This behavior improves the navigation experience by maintaining UI state (form inputs, or expanded sections) when users navigate back and forth between routes.
55	
56	> **Good to know**: Next.js uses heuristics to keep a few recently visited routes `"hidden"`, while older routes are removed from the DOM to prevent excessive growth.
57	
58	Some UI patterns behave differently when components stay mounted instead of unmounting. See the [Preserving UI state guide](/docs/app/guides/preserving-ui-state) for handling common patterns like dropdowns, dialogs, and testing.
59	
60	## Version History
61	
62	| Version | Change                                                                                                                            |
63	| ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
64	| 16.0.0  | `cacheComponents` introduced. This flag controls the `ppr`, `useCache`, and `dynamicIO` flags as a single, unified configuration. |
65

The first call with a given set of inputs runs the function body and stores its output. Every later call with the same inputs reuses that output, within a render pass and across requests, for as long as the entry lasts. 112 113 Outputs are stored by a [cache handler](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers), [in memory](#runtime-caching-considerations) by default, and last until they [revalidate](#revalidation). 114 115 ```tsx filename="lib/orders.ts" 116 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 117 118 export async function getOrderSummary(accountId: string) { 119 'use cache' 120 cacheLife('hours') 121 122 const orders = await getOrders(accountId) 123 const totals = await getOrderTotals(accountId) 124 125 return { orders, totals } 126 } 127 128 export async function getOrders(accountId: string) { 129 'use cache' 130 cacheLife('hours') 131 132 return db.orders.findMany({ where: { accountId } }) 133 } 134 135 export async function getOrderTotals(accountId: string) { 136 return db.orders.aggregate({ where: { accountId }, _sum: { amount: true } }) 137 } 138 ``` 139 140 In the example above, each `accountId` has its own entry for `getOrderSummary`, holding the serialized `{ orders, totals }` object it returns. If an earlier call, through the summary or directly, already filled one, `db.orders.findMany` doesn't run and those orders become part of the summary's output. See [nested caching behavior](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#nested-caching-behavior) for how an inner lifetime affects the entry around it. 141 142 Note that `getOrderTotals` is not cached. It is exported so other parts of the application can read fresh totals in an uncached scope. The following constraints ensure cache behavior remains predictable and secure. 238 239 ### Request-time APIs 240 241 Cached functions and components **cannot** access runtime APIs like `cookies()`, `headers()`, or `searchParams`, and the restriction follows the call stack: a helper the cached function calls that reads one of these fails the same way, with the [`next-request-in-use-cache`](/docs/messages/next-request-in-use-cache) error. On a dynamically rendered route this surfaces when the route runs, so it can pass `next build` and fail under `next start`. Read these values outside the cached scope and pass them as arguments. 242 243 ### Runtime caching considerations 244 245 While `use cache` is designed primarily to include uncached data in the static shell, it can also cache data at runtime using in-memory LRU (Least Recently Used) storage. 246 247 With the default in-memory handler, runtime cache behavior depends on your hosting environment: 248 249 | Environment | Runtime Caching Behavior | 250 | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | 251 | **Serverless** | Cache entries typically don't persist across requests (each request can be a different instance), or during revalidation. Build-time caching works normally. | 252 | **Self-hosted** | Cache entries persist across requests. Control cache size with [`cacheMaxMemorySize`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheMaxMemorySize). | 253 254 For example, in a serverless environment, a cached function shared by two pages executes on each static shell revalidation, whereas in self-hosted or environments with persistent memory, the cached output is reused if it's still fresh. 255 256 If the default in-memory cache isn't enough, consider **[`use cache: remote`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote)** which allows platforms to provide a dedicated cache handler (like Redis or KV database). This helps reduce hits against data sources not scaled to your total traffic, though it comes with costs (storage, network latency, platform fees). 257 258 > [!NOTE] 259 > With the default in-memory handler, serverless instances are ephemeral, so entries may not be reused between requests, unlike with `use cache: remote`. Values stored via `React.cache` outside a `use cache` function are not visible inside it. 292 293 This means you cannot use `React.cache` to pass data into a `use cache` scope: 294 295 ```tsx 296 import { cache } from 'react' 297 298 const store = cache(() => ({ current: null as string | null })) 299 300 function Parent() { 301 const shared = store() 302 shared.current = 'value from parent' 303 return 304 } 305 306 async function Child() { 307 'use cache' 308 const shared = store() 309 // shared.current is null, not 'value from parent' 310 // use cache has its own isolated React.cache scope 311 return

To pass data into a `use cache` scope, use function arguments instead. 316 317 ## `use cache` at runtime 318 319 On the **server**, cache entries are stored in-memory and respect the `revalidate` and `expire` times from your `cacheLife` configuration. You can customize the cache storage by configuring [`cacheHandlers`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers) in your `next.config.js` file. 320 321 On the **client**, content from the server cache is stored in the browser's memory for the duration defined by the `stale` time. The client router enforces a **minimum 30-second stale time**, regardless of configuration. 322 323 The `x-nextjs-stale-time` response header communicates cache lifetime from server to client, ensuring coordinated behavior. 324 325 ## Revalidation 326 327 Cached functions revalidate based on the `revalidate` and `expire` times in their `cacheLife` profile, or on-demand through tags. These two approaches are not mutually exclusive and are often paired: 328 329 - **[Time-based](#time-based-revalidation)**: refresh automatically after a set duration with [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife). 330 - **[On-demand](#on-demand-revalidation)**: invalidate after a mutation with [`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) and [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) or [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag). 331 332 For example, a blog post that changes only when its author edits it can use a long `cacheLife` like `max` with a `cacheTag`, then invalidate on demand when the post is saved.
